The curse took his family — his children are temporal echoes in the Shifting Nursery — and his grief has expressed itself as manic energy, ceaseless activity, and an absolute refusal to sit still or be quiet, because silence means thinking about what he has lost. He is the physical powerhouse of the cursed trio and can be a formidable combat ally if the party earns his trust.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Everything the March Hare does is driven by one thing: getting back to his children. His mania is a coping mechanism for unbearable loss. He will do anything, fight anything, and sacrifice anything to break the curse and hold his children again. Earning his trust requires acknowledging his grief — not as madness, but as love expressed in the only way left available to him.

npcsInvolved.name: The Dormouse
npcsInvolved.description: A mouse the size of a large dog, perpetually asleep inside an enormous teapot. Its fur is the color of chamomile tea and it smells faintly of honey and old dreams. The Dormouse is the most powerful entity in the Tea Quarter — its dreams sustain the district's existence and provide the only pathway to the Temporal Sanctum where Time resides. It speaks in sleep-mumbles that are accidentally prophetic, narrating events in a dreamy third-person ('And then the brave adventurers found the gear, or perhaps the gear found them, it's hard to say really...') that occasionally provides crucial information wrapped in whimsy.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The Dormouse does not have conventional motivation — it is primarily asleep. However, its dreams are shaped by a deep, unconscious desire to fix the broken time in the Tea Quarter. Its Dreamscape creates pathways to the solutions the party needs, as if the Dormouse is trying to help from within its sleep. When (if) it finally wakes after the curse breaks, it reveals that it has been aware the entire time — it chose to keep sleeping because its dreams were the only thing keeping the Tea Quarter from collapsing entirely. It sacrificed its waking life to sustain everyone else's. Its first waking words should reflect quiet, sleepy heroism.

rewards.story: The party has broken the eternal curse on the Mad Tea Quarter, healing the wounded Avatar of Time through the power of a genuine apology. The Hatter's genius is restored, the March Hare is reunited with his family, and the Dormouse can finally wake from its decades-long vigil. The Tea Quarter blooms back to life, and the party earns the eternal gratitude of its inhabitants. The Temporal Gear, imbued with Time's own gratitude, is a critical component for the campaign's final scenario. The party has also learned a fundamental truth about Wonderland: words have literal power here, and the bravest thing one can do is take responsibility for the damage careless words can cause.

twists: The curse is not a punishment but a wound — Time is not angry, Time is hurt. The Hatter's careless words during his performance ('I could murder Time') had literal power in Wonderland and genuinely injured a living, sentient being. The entire eternal tea party is Time's scream of pain, not its act of vengeance.

The Time Elemental in the Clock Tower is a fragment of the Hatter's own temporal essence, torn from him by the curse. Destroying it would permanently damage the Hatter's mind. It must be weakened and bypassed, not killed.

The March Hare is not mad — he is grieving. His manic behavior is a coping mechanism for the loss of his children, who are trapped as temporal echoes in the Shifting Nursery. His madness is love with nowhere to go.

The Dormouse is the secret hero of the Tea Quarter — it has been consciously maintaining its sleep for decades because its dreams are the only thing preventing the time-frozen Quarter from collapsing into temporal chaos. It sacrificed its waking life to save everyone else.

The Queen of Hearts deliberately sabotaged the Hatter's performance for Time, knowing his words would wound Time and trigger the curse. The Tea Quarter's suffering is partially her fault — a thread that connects to the campaign's final scenario.

The curse can only be broken by combining mechanical restoration (the four clock gears) with emotional resolution (a genuine apology). Doing only one creates a temporary fix — the clock ticks to 6:01 but stops again within days. Both solutions must be achieved for a permanent cure.
dmTips: The temporal loop mechanic is this scenario's signature feature — use it creatively. If the party loses a combat encounter, consider having the loop reset: the party retains their knowledge of the fight (enemy tactics, terrain, etc.) but positions and HP reset. This gives players a 'Groundhog Day' experience that is both mechanically forgiving and narratively interesting. Limit this to 1-2 resets per encounter to avoid tedium.

The tea party etiquette challenge is the most complex social encounter in the scenario. Prepare a list of 6-8 Wonderland etiquette rules before the session (examples: never ask for more tea, always accept what is offered even if impossible, answer riddles with non-answers, never sit in a clean seat, compliment the March Hare's butter, never mention what time it is). Reveal rules one at a time as the party encounters them, and apply fey consequences (polymorph, shrinking, rhyme-curse) with a light touch — they should be funny and inconvenient, not devastating.

The March Hare's grief reveal in the Shifting Nursery is the scenario's emotional peak. Do not rush it. Give the players time to react, and let the March Hare's vulnerability land. If a player's character has a backstory involving family loss, draw a parallel. This scene should make the curse feel personal, not just mechanical.

The Avatar of Time should be played as genuinely sympathetic even during combat. Its attacks are defensive, not predatory. It begs the party to stop hurting it even as it fights back. If a player pauses mid-combat to attempt diplomacy, reward this immediately with a reduced DC or a hint about what the apology needs to contain. The ideal resolution involves BOTH combat and diplomacy — the party fights Time to a standstill, then puts down their weapons and talks.

Stuttering initiative is a signature temporal mechanic: at the start of each round in combat encounters within the Tea Quarter, roll a d6. On a 1-2, all initiative counts are rerolled. On a 3-4, the top and bottom of the initiative order swap. On a 5-6, initiative proceeds normally. This creates tactical uncertainty that reinforces the broken-time theme. Drop this mechanic once the curse is broken.

The Hatter's riddles should always contain genuine clues disguised as nonsense. If you are struggling to improvise riddles, use this formula: take the actual information the party needs, rephrase it as a question, then answer the question with a different question. Example: if the party needs to know the gear is in the Butter Workshop, the Hatter might say 'What goes best with time? Butter, naturally. And what goes best with butter? Everything, if you're mad enough to look.'

Track the four clock gears carefully. Gear #1 is in the Butter Workshop, Gear #2 is in the Half Room, Gear #3 is in the Clock Tower's Pendulum Hall, and Gear #4 is in the Dormouse's Dreamscape. The party can recover them in any order except #4, which requires the Hatter's help to access the Dreamscape. If the party tries to install gears before having all four, the clock mechanism partially activates but cannot sustain itself — time flickers forward for a few seconds, giving the party a tantalizing glimpse of the curse breaking before the mechanism stalls.

For the Dormouse's Dreamscape, embrace dream logic fully. Let players attempt anything if they believe in it strongly enough (Wisdom DC 15 to maintain belief). Flying, walking through walls, summoning objects from memory — all are possible here if the player commits to the fiction. This rewards creative, confident play and makes the Dreamscape feel genuinely different from the rest of the scenario.
